newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-- Jobless claims to set tone.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-- Jobless claims to set tone.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices were seen holding in tight ranges on Thursday as dealers had little data scheduled before the Federal Reserve's policy-making meeting next week.

Initial jobless claims, slated for release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, were seen as the most important reading of the session. Economists polled by Reuters expected claims to fall to 340,000 from 347,000 in the prior week. Due at the same time was the APICS survey for June, and at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT the Conference Board's help wanted index for May.

The Treasury sold $11.5 billion of five-year notes on Wednesday, and the auction was considered quite strong with the notes fetching a better-than-expected 6.298 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio was 3.19 and noncompetitive bids were at $549 million.
"We don't have a lot in the way of numbers. Claims will be the most important (data)," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Any surprises in claims -- especially lower -- could send bond prices lower, he said, as labor market tightness continues to worry fixed-income investors.
Moran said the tone of the market could continue to be affected by fears of higher Japanese interest rates following the robust Tankan report on manufacturing activity on Wednesday.
Japanese interest rates have been suppressed for quite a while in an effort to jump-start a sagging economy, but thus far the effort has had little effect.
David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International, said the four-month average for initial claims had been moving up for the past two weeks.
"This suggests some softening in the job market, but the general news is that the job market is tightening," Resler said.
"Other than initial claims the market looks to the FOMC and the employment report (next week)," said Michael Englund, economist with MMS International.

He said gross domestic product on Friday should see a $5 billion loss in inventories offset by a $6 billion gain in exports. Englund said another tightening probably would not occur in July. He said there already was seen renewed strength in the manufacturing sector.
Dan Seto, economist with Nikko Securities International, said Wednesday's action may set the tone for Thursday's trading session.
He saw initial unemployment claims holding in recent ranges and help wanted claims falling -- putting the bond market on the defensive.
Still, he expected prices to remain range bound before next week's FOMC meeting.
"There's still a strong expectation that the Fed will not move (to tighten) in July," Seto said.
Late Wednesday, the Treasury's 30-year bond was trading at 98-20/32, down 15/32, to yield 6.73 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum the three-month bill rate was down two basis points at 4.99 percent. Six-month bills were down five one basis points at 5.03 percent and year-bills were unchanged at 5.34 percent.
Five-year notes were down 3/32 at 100-24/32, yielding 6.32 percent. Ten-year notes were down 7/32 at 101-11/32, yielding 6.44 percent.
